facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The 37.19 m high 9-storied tower is one of the most remarkable in India.
facts.text: The Vijaya Stambha inside Chittorgarh Fort is an imposing nine-storey monument measuring 37.19 metres in height.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: There are around 157 narrow steps leading to the terrace from where one can have a beautiful view of Chittorgarh town and the fort.
facts.text: An internal spiral staircase comprising 157 steps leads through the nine storeys to the upper terrace of the Vijaya Stambha.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The tower was constructed by the Hindu Rajput king Rana Kumbha of Mewar in 1448 CE to commemorate his victory over the army of Sultanate of Malwa led by Mahmud Khilji in the Battle of Sarangpur.
facts.text: Maharana Kumbha completed the construction of the Vijaya Stambha around 1448 CE to commemorate his victory over the Malwa Sultanate at the Battle of Sarangpur.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The names of the architect, Sutradhar Jaita and his three sons who assisted him, Napa, Puja, and Poma, are carved on the fifth floor of the tower.
facts.text: An epigraphic inscription on the fifth storey of the Vijaya Stambha identifies master architect Sutradhar Jaita and his three sons Napa, Puja, and Poma.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Ratnasimha is attested by the 1302 CE (1359 VS) Dariba temple inscription, which records a gift of 16 drammas (coins) to the temple during his reign.
facts.text: The historical ruler Rawal Ratnasimha of Mewar is attested by an epigraph dated to 1302 CE at the Dariba temple.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Padmavat is an epic poem written in 1540 CE by Sufi poet Malik Muhammad Jayasi, who wrote it in the Hindustani language of Awadhi.
facts.text: The Sufi poet Malik Muhammad Jayasi composed the Awadhi romance Padmavat around 1540 CE, introducing the earliest surviving narrative featuring Queen Padmavati.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Jayasi explains the allegory in the concluding verses: Chittor represents the body, the king the mind, Simhala the heart, and Padmini wisdom.
facts.text: In the concluding verses of Padmavat, Jayasi explains that Chittor allegorically represents the human body, the king denotes the mind, and Padmini represents wisdom.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Ratansen dies in a duel with Devpal, the king of Kumbhalner; subsequently, Padmini and Nagmati commit sati on Ratansen's funeral pyre before Alauddin reaches the fort.
facts.text: In Jayasi's epic poem, King Ratansen is killed in single combat against King Devpal of Kumbhalner rather than by the imperial army besieging the fort.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: Most modern historians have rejected the authenticity of the Padmini legend, viewing her as an allegorical creation, while some traditional scholars argue the poem adapted older Mewari oral lore.
facts.source_name: The Many Lives of a Rajput Queen
facts.text: Historians disagree on whether Rani Padmini was an authentic historical figure preserved through Mewari oral traditions or a literary invention first created by Jayasi in 1540 CE.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: The popular story says that when Khilji attacked Chittor, he fell for Padmini on seeing her reflection in the mirror, a trope absent from the earliest texts.
facts.text: A popular regional folklore claims that the Delhi sultan was granted a glimpse of Rani Padmini's face reflected across a series of mirrors in her water palace.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: Amir Khusrau described the jauhar at Ranthambore in 1301 CE, where Rajput women threw themselves into a fire when defeat was imminent.
facts.text: The earliest contemporary Sultanate chronicle documenting the rite of Jauhar describes the 1301 CE siege of Ranthambore rather than Chittor.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: While fourteenth-century Persian sources make no mention of a jauhar at Chittor in 1303, later Rajput traditions and sixteenth-century chronicles assert that the women committed mass self-immolation.
facts.text: Scholars disagree over whether a mass Jauhar took place during the 1303 CE siege of Chittorgarh, as primary fourteenth-century Sultanate sources omit it while sixteenth-century Rajput and Persian chronicles describe it as fact.
